title: Ravens explode for 41 points in Minter’s debut, but how serious are injuries to Flowers and Lane?
author: James Boyd
content:
INDIANAPOLIS — The Baltimore Ravens exploded for 31 first-half points en route to a 41-23 win over the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday in coach Jesse Minter’s debut.

The Ravens scored touchdowns on four of their first five possessions, as 30-year-old offensive coordinator Declan Doyle torched the Colts’ defense in his first game as a play caller. Wide receiver Zay Flowers led the way for Baltimore (five receptions for a career-high 150 yards and a touchdown) before exiting with a hamstring injury before halftime.

Baltimore’s receiving group took another hit when third-round rookie Ja’Kobi Lane was ruled out with a wrist injury, but the Colts had no answer for the Ravens’ rushing attack. Derrick Henry rumbled for 144 yards and three scores — passing Marcus Allen for third in NFL history with 125 career rushing touchdowns.

Indianapolis quarterback Daniel Jones got off to a near-perfect start in his return from a torn Achilles, marching the Colts down the field for an opening-drive touchdown. It was largely a struggle from there: Jones finished 19-for-31 passing for 166 yards, one touchdown and one interception.

A telling sequence came in the second quarter when the Ravens, already leading 14-6, faced a fourth-and-goal from the 3-yard line. Minter decided to go for it. The Ravens didn’t convert, but that was a show of faith in the offense and probably a testament to the attacking, aggressive style Minter wants to be known for. Minter has plenty to fix. The Ravens had a big turnover that got the Colts back in the game in the second quarter, and Baltimore was prone to penalties, particularly on offense. The Ravens’ defense also didn’t close the game as forcefully as Minter probably would have liked. However, I think you saw the type of aggressive, dangerous team Minter wants them to be. — Jeff Zrebiec, Ravens beat writer

Doyle was certainly aggressive and had some interesting wrinkles. On Flowers’ 54-yard touchdown catch, the wide receiver started the play lined up in the backfield. On the Ravens’ first touchdown, a five-yard Lamar Jackson run, Doyle had a left tackle lined up on the right side, with pass-catching tight end Mark Andrews in a blocking position. Doyle utilized “11” personnel more frequently than his predecessor. Jackson was also lined up under center far more often. The general theme, though, is Doyle hunting explosive plays and Jackson looking plenty comfortable in running the show. — Zrebiec

Honestly, everything, after Indy gave up 506 yards of total offense.

Indy’s secondary was supposed to be the strength of its defense, so the fact that Jackson didn’t log his first incompletion until there were 38 seconds left in the first quarter was a red flag. Fittingly, after that first incompletion forced the Ravens into a third-and-12 from the Colts’ 47-yard line, Jackson found Flowers for an 18-yard first-down catch to keep the Ravens’ drive alive. Colts cornerback Justin Walley was matched often with Flowers early on, and Flowers gave Walley, who missed his entire rookie season because of a torn ACL, plenty of welcome-to-the-league moments during his NFL debut Sunday.

Indy cut veteran Kenny Moore II, who was poised to play a reduced role this year, because the team believed Walley was a better option as its starting nickelback. However, that decision looked like it backfired Sunday. What’s more, the rest of Indy’s heralded secondary hardly made any plays as its All-Pro tandem of outside cornerbacks, Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward Sr., were essentially afterthoughts in a dominant performance from Jackson.

Not to be overlooked, the Colts’ run defense was terrible, too. Henry totaled 24 carries for 144 yards and three touchdowns, marking his 56th 100-yard rushing game. — James Boyd, Colts beat writer

Where’s the pressure? I mean, outside Laiatu Latu and Arden Key’s combined sack on Jackson that caused a fumble, this was an embarrassment for the Colts’ front. Jackson had time to throw to his receivers, who racked up yards and gashed the secondary (and, sheesh, don’t get me started on Ward, Walley and Cam Bynum today). And of course, Henry was vintage in getting downhill and bullying every player who got in his way. The Colts lack an intimidating, game-changing force up front, and it’s going to hurt them this year.— Candace Buckner, columnist

The big-picture takeaway is that nothing looked wrong with Jones’ mechanics. Just nine months removed from rupturing his right Achilles tendon, Jones proved he was fully healthy Sunday as he maneuvered around the pocket and even had a four-yard scramble. It also sounds simple, but the fact that he got up after every hit was encouraging after Jones didn’t play in the preseason and therefore hadn’t taken a hit since last year.

But beyond Jones’ overall health, the Indianapolis offense was stagnant after a surgical first drive. Colts coach Shane Steichen is known as one of the best opening-drive play callers in the league, and Jones led the team on a nine-play, 65-yard drive to start. Jones, however, was picked off on Indy’s second drive by Ravens linebacker Roquan Smith, and the Colts’ next four drives resulted in the following: punt, punt, lost fumble and punt.

Obviously, the Colts’ poor offensive showing wasn’t all Jones. The team’s top pass catchers, particularly wide receiver Alec Pierce and tight end Tyler Warren, were nonfactors against Baltimore’s defense and didn’t come alive until late in the second half when the game was already out of reach. And Keenan Allen, the six-time Pro Bowl receiver Indy signed last month, had just six catches for 32 yards. — Boyd

This is a big concern coming out of this game for the Ravens. They were already relatively thin at the position heading into this season, and then they lost Flowers (hamstring) and Lane (wrist) to injuries. By game’s end, they had only three wide receivers left: Rashod Bateman, return specialist LaJohntay Wester and veteran Chris Moore, who was elevated from the practice squad for the game primarily to provide special teams help.

Wide receiver Devontez Walker (groin) is nearing a return, and the Ravens could move rookie fourth-round pick Elijah Surratt into the lineup, but neither of them started the season as top three receivers like Flowers and Lane were. If both Flowers and Lane are headed for lengthy absences, the Ravens may have to bring somebody in, but right now, they probably have enough in-house to get by for a few weeks.

“I have confidence in my guys who stepped in,” Jackson said about the Ravens’ depleted receiving corps. “Chris Moore, [LaJohntay Wester], those guys stepped in and just did a great job. We kept the offense rolling. We just got a great group of guys, and that’s what they preach. You never know when the next guy is going to be up, so just dial in in practice, stay locked in, and you never know when your number is going to be called. Those guys showed up today.” — Zrebiec
